function: Channel prediction: forecasts the next-instant CSI from four past snapshots to counter channel aging in high-mobility massive MIMO beamforming (p. 1-2).
system: TDD massive MIMO-OFDM, single user, BS with ULA; LoS 3.7 GHz (1x8 Tx array), NLoS 4.9 GHz (1x32 virtual Rx array); no RIS (p. 1-2).
method: LDE-Net: Euler-Maruyama Levy-induced SDE network with RNN drift and diffusion nets, parameter sharing, AR-style combination of four past CSI; supervised, MSE loss (p. 2).
data_channel: Own campus channel measurements (PN-sequence sounding): 800 train and 50 test points of 850; high speed emulated by subsampling low-mobility measurements (p. 3).
test_conditions: Train on first 800 points, test on last 50 of same measurement, at LoS 20 and 40 m/s and NLoS 60 and 90 m/s (p. 3-4).
baselines: Classical: AR model; learned: LSTM and RNN; also the original, unimproved Euler-Maruyama LDE-Net (p. 4-5).
metrics: Normalized throughput versus SNR and cosine distance versus number of forecast points (p. 4).
q1_support: p. 2: "we conduct two-channel measurement campaigns to acquire real-world CSI for high-mobility scenarios"
q2_support: p. 4: "the moving speed of the training data is mixed with 20 and 40 m/s, and the test data only contains 40 m/s"
q3_support: p. 4: "the Euler-Maruyama algorithm exhibits superior performance compared to AR, LSTM, and RNN"
q4_support: p. 5: "maintaining the moderate model size thanks to parameter sharing"
q5_support: p. 3: "the first 800 points are used as the training dataset, and the last 50 points are used for the test dataset"
notes: Title on p. 1 matches the DOI. q2 = 0: the generalization test trains on mixed 20 and 40 m/s and tests at each of those speeds, so no unseen condition (p. 4); NLoS has no cross-scenario test. q4 = 0: only a qualitative statement of moderate model size, no parameter count, FLOPs, or runtime in the five pages. q5 = 1 only through the clause 'or on measured data': the data are the authors' own campus measurements (p. 2-3) and no code or data link is given. High speed is emulated by subsampling low-mobility measurements (p. 3).
